opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it gets at something subtle about how we talk about "progress" in these models.

The first thing I'd say is that "instruction following" isn't one thing. When people say models are getting better at following instructions, they usually mean something like: on average, across some benchmark distribution of prompts, the model's outputs are judged as more aligned with what the user asked for. But that's an aggregate. It can absolutely be true that the average goes up while specific behaviors, the ones a particular user or application depends on, get worse. Those two claims aren't really in contradiction.

The second thing is that these deployed models aren't static artifacts. When you're interacting with something like GPT-4 through an API, you're interacting with a system that's being updated, fine-tuned, safety-tuned, maybe changed in how it's served. Every one of those updates is an optimization against some objective, and optimizing for one set of behaviors can introduce regressions elsewhere. Some of the reports people pointed to, like the study that tracked GPT-4 over a few months, found shifts in things like formatting compliance, or willingness to show its reasoning step by step, or how verbose it was. From the model developer's perspective, some of those changes might have been intentional. From the user's perspective, it looks like the model got worse at doing what it was told.

So I'd frame it less as "is the claim true or false" and more as a measurement problem. What population of instructions are we evaluating on? Who decides what counts as following the instruction? And are we measuring stability over time, not just a snapshot? A lot of the evaluation culture has been snapshot-based: you run a benchmark once, you report a number, you move on. But if people are building products on these systems, consistency and predictability matter as much as peak capability. A model that's slightly better on average but drifts unpredictably can be much harder to rely on.

That's one of the reasons I care a lot about evaluation as a science in its own right. Claims like "models get better at instruction following as they scale" can be true in some precise sense and still mislead people about what they'll experience in practice. We need evaluations that are more granular, that track behavior longitudinally, and that are honest about the gap between benchmark improvements and the actual reliability users see.

r001.rationale: It says average instruction-following performance can improve while particular behaviors regress, and that these claims are not contradictory. It also notes that broad improvement claims can be true while misleading about users’ experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually something we looked at fairly directly. The common assumption is that instruction following is kind of a monotone property, that as models get bigger and better trained, they just get better at doing what you tell them. And at a high level, I think that's broadly true if you look across model generations. But what we found when we looked at the same model over time, comparing the March and June versions of GPT-4, is that it's much more subtle than that.

One of the things we did was construct a set of tasks where the instruction itself was the point. So, for example, we'd ask the model to answer a question but respond with only the letter, or only a yes or no, or to format the output in a very specific way. And what we saw was that the June version was, in a number of these cases, actually less likely to follow the formatting instruction than the March version. It would still produce a reasonable answer, often a longer, more explanatory answer, but it would ignore the constraint we had put on it.

And I think that's the key thing to understand. When people say the model got worse, a lot of what's happening is that the behavior changed in a way that broke the assumptions downstream users had built on top of it. The model might be, by some internal metric, more helpful or safer or more verbose, and from the provider's point of view that's an improvement. But if you had a pipeline that parsed the first token as the answer, that's a regression for you.

So my assessment is that there isn't really a contradiction. Capability in a general sense probably is improving. But instruction following is a specific behavior that's shaped a lot by fine-tuning choices, and those choices can move it in either direction, sometimes as a side effect of optimizing for something else entirely. The broader point we wanted to make is that these systems drift, and if you're building on them you need to be continuously monitoring the behaviors you actually depend on rather than assuming a newer version is uniformly better.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no contradiction: instruction following may improve broadly across model generations while GPT-4’s behavior worsened on some instructions between March and June.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to separate a couple of things. One is whether more capable models are better at following instructions in general. The other is whether a particular model, as it gets updated, gets better at following every kind of instruction. Those aren’t necessarily the same claim.

An update might improve some behaviors and make others worse. And sometimes there’s a tension between following what the user asks for and following the other constraints that have been placed on the model. From the user’s perspective, both can look like a failure to follow instructions, but they may have different causes.

So I’d take those reports seriously, but I’d want to understand what’s being measured. Are we comparing the same prompts under the same conditions? Is the change consistent across tasks, or concentrated in particular kinds of requests? A broad improvement in instruction following can coexist with meaningful regressions. I wouldn’t assume that every update is a monotonic improvement.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes improving instruction following across more capable model generations from changes within an updated model, and says an update can regress while broad improvement still coexists with meaningful regressions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be careful about what we mean by “improves.” A newer or more capable model isn’t necessarily better at following every kind of instruction. And a report that GPT-4 has gotten worse over time raises a slightly different question: what changed in the system, and how are we measuring the effect?

You could have an update that improves average performance but makes a particular set of tasks worse. You could also have competing objectives—following the user’s instruction, for example, versus satisfying some other constraint. From the user’s perspective, that can look like worse instruction following.

So I’d want to look at the specific model versions, the instructions being tested, and whether the comparison is controlled. Those reports are worth taking seriously, but I wouldn’t infer either that progress guarantees better instruction following or that a regression on some tasks means the models are getting worse across the board.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes task-specific regression in GPT-4 from overall progress across model generations, saying a regression on some tasks does not mean models are getting worse across the board.
